solutions.text: Phần A

1. Several cities are trialling AUTONOMOUS VEHICLES, hoping to cut down on accidents caused by driver error. --- AUTONOMOUS VEHICLES (noun phrase, plural) = xe tự lái; collocation: "fully autonomous vehicles", "trial autonomous vehicles"; lưu ý "autonomous" là tính từ, không viết "autonomy vehicle".

2. A new metro line could help ALLEVIATE the traffic problem in the capital, though it probably won't solve it completely. --- ALLEVIATE (verb) = làm giảm bớt (không phải loại bỏ hoàn toàn); collocation: "alleviate congestion/the pressure/a problem"; không nhầm với "eliminate".

3. After years of staying in the same job, she felt a growing sense of WANDERLUST, so she quit and bought a one-way ticket. --- WANDERLUST (noun, uncountable) = khao khát du lịch mãnh liệt; collocation: "a sense of wanderlust", "satisfy your wanderlust"; không dùng "a wanderlust" theo nghĩa đếm được.

4. In cities with proper cycle lanes, riding a bike is becoming a VIABLE alternative to driving to work. --- VIABLE (adjective) = khả thi, thực tế; collocation: "a viable alternative/option", "economically viable"; dễ nhầm chính tả với "visible".

5. The AVIATION industry has faced growing pressure to explain its large share of global carbon emissions. --- AVIATION (noun, uncountable) = ngành hàng không; collocation: "the aviation industry", "civil aviation"; chỉ ngành nói chung, không dùng cho một chuyến bay cụ thể.

6. Without continued investment in transport INFRASTRUCTURE, a country's economy will struggle to remain competitive in the long run. --- INFRASTRUCTURE (noun, uncountable) = hạ tầng; collocation: "transport infrastructure", "invest in infrastructure"; không có dạng số nhiều "infrastructures".

7. New rules are forcing car manufacturers to cut vehicle EMISSIONS released by their exhaust pipes. --- EMISSIONS (noun, plural) = khí thải; collocation: "cut/reduce vehicle emissions", "carbon emissions"; thường dùng số nhiều khi nói chung về khí thải phương tiện.

8. Drivers entering the city centre now have to pay a CONGESTION CHARGE designed specifically to discourage unnecessary car journeys during the day. --- CONGESTION CHARGE (noun phrase) = phí ùn tắc; collocation: "introduce/pay a congestion charge", "congestion charge zone"; luôn viết "charge" số ít dù áp dụng cho nhiều xe.

9. Local authorities are promoting SUSTAINABLE MOBILITY that meets people's needs today without damaging the environment for future generations. --- SUSTAINABLE MOBILITY (noun phrase) = giao thông bền vững; collocation: "promote/invest in sustainable mobility", "a sustainable mobility plan".

10. Bike-sharing schemes have quickly GAINED significant TRACTION in several major cities over the past few years. --- GAIN TRACTION (verbal phrase) = bắt đầu được ưa chuộng/chấp nhận; collocation: "gain significant traction", "fail to gain traction"; nghĩa bóng, không liên quan đến ma sát vật lý.

11. Whenever planners widen a motorway, the extra space triggers INDUCED DEMAND, with new traffic filling the gap almost immediately. --- INDUCED DEMAND (noun phrase) = nhu cầu phát sinh; collocation: "the theory of induced demand", "a classic case of induced demand"; hiện tượng mở đường lại kéo theo xe cộ tăng thêm.

12. Rather than visiting the usual crowded tourist spots, more travellers are now choosing destinations OFF THE BEATEN TRACK. --- OFF THE BEATEN TRACK (idiom) = xa xôi, ít người biết đến; collocation: "explore/venture off the beaten track", "a destination off the beaten track"; cụm cố định, không chia động từ.
Phần B

1. Band 6: We should use public transport more to reduce pollution. - Band 7: Making greater use of public transport would help to reduce pollution levels in cities. - Band 8: A shift towards sustainable mobility is essential if cities are to curb harmful vehicle emissions in any meaningful way.

2. Band 6: Traffic jams waste a lot of people's time every day. - Band 7: Traffic congestion causes many commuters to lose a significant amount of time each day. - Band 8: Rush-hour gridlock imposes substantial economic costs and erodes commuters' quality of life far more than most people realise.

3. Band 6: Building more roads does not always solve traffic problems. - Band 7: Expanding road networks does not necessarily ease congestion in the long term. - Band 8: Owing to induced demand, widening motorways tends to generate fresh traffic rather than alleviating the very congestion it was meant to relieve.

4. Band 6: Charging drivers to enter the city centre could reduce traffic there. - Band 7: Introducing a congestion charge could discourage unnecessary car journeys into the city centre. - Band 8: Introducing a congestion charge has proven, in cities that have dared to implement one, an effective if politically contentious means of easing inner-city gridlock.

5. Band 6: Governments need to spend more money on trains and buses. - Band 7: Greater investment in rail and bus infrastructure is needed to improve public transport. - Band 8: Sustained investment in transport infrastructure is indispensable to long-term economic competitiveness, however politically unglamorous such spending may seem.

6. Band 6: Self-driving cars might make roads safer in the future. - Band 7: Autonomous vehicles could potentially reduce road accidents caused by human error. - Band 8: Should autonomous vehicles achieve widespread adoption, accident rates attributable to human error could fall dramatically within a generation.

7. Band 6: Closing streets to cars can make city centres nicer places to be. - Band 7: Pedestrianising city streets can make urban centres more pleasant and liveable. - Band 8: Pedestrianising city centres can revitalise public space and reduce reliance on private vehicles, contrary to retailers' fears of falling revenue.

8. Band 6: Air travel produces a lot of pollution and this is hard to solve. - Band 7: The aviation industry generates considerable emissions that are notoriously difficult to reduce. - Band 8: Decarbonising aviation remains one of the thorniest challenges in climate policy, given the industry's continued reliance on carbon-intensive fuel.

passages.text: In late 2016, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology launched an online experiment called the Moral Machine. Participants were asked to choose between unpalatable outcomes for a self-driving vehicle: should the algorithm steer toward an elderly pedestrian or three young passengers, a doctor or a homeless person, a child or a pregnant woman. By the time the experiment closed, it had logged more than forty million responses from 233 countries. The results were widely reported as evidence that ethical preferences for autonomous vehicles vary by region. Yet the lead researcher, Iyad Rahwan, has since cautioned that the data tell a less dramatic story. The cross-national variation was real but modest, and the framing of the choices, as descendants of the philosopher Philippa Foot's "trolley problem", may have steered the public debate in a direction the engineering reality does not warrant.

The engineering reality, according to Heather Roff, a roboticist formerly at Oxford, is that fully autonomous vehicles almost never face a clean binary choice. A self-driving car operating in a city encounters tens of thousands of micro-decisions per hour, the great majority of which concern lane discipline, gap acceptance and following distance rather than trolley-style dilemmas. Where catastrophic choices do arise, they tend to emerge from a chain of upstream errors, such as misclassified objects or degraded sensor fusion, rather than from a deliberate weighing of human lives. The implication, Roff argues, is that designing an ethical algorithm in advance may be less consequential than auditing the perception stack that feeds it, although both layers ultimately matter.

A second strand of research has shifted the conversation from individual ethics to systemic design. Mobility-as-a-Service, often abbreviated as MaaS, treats urban transport not as a portfolio of separate modes but as a single subscription. A traveller opens a smartphone application, types a destination, and is offered an integrated route that may combine a tram, a shared bicycle, an autonomous shuttle and a short walk. The Finnish operator Whim launched the first commercial MaaS bundle in Helsinki in 2016. Subsequent studies, including a 2021 evaluation by the urban-transport economist Maria Kamargianni at University College London, found that subscribers reduced private-car trips by between fifteen and twenty-eight per cent over the first eighteen months. The effect, however, was concentrated among households with at least one car already, suggesting that MaaS may discourage marginal trips rather than eliminate vehicle ownership.

Whether autonomous technology will accelerate MaaS or undermine it remains contested. Proponents argue that driverless shuttles could reduce the per-trip cost of shared mobility to a level at which private ownership ceases to make economic sense, particularly for low-mileage households. The transport historian Peter Norton, however, has noted a recurring pattern in twentieth-century mobility history: each round of efficiency gain has tended to be absorbed by additional consumption, a phenomenon transport economists describe as induced demand. If autonomous vehicles make travel cheaper and less effortful, total kilometres travelled may rise even as the per-kilometre footprint falls. The carbon implications, on this reading, are far from automatic.

Ethics intrudes again at the level of data. A MaaS subscription generates a fine-grained record of when, where and with whom a traveller moves. Anna Nikolaeva, a mobility scholar at the University of Amsterdam, has argued that these traces are themselves a form of currency, traded between platform operators, municipal authorities and insurers in ways that subscribers seldom understand. The European Mobility Data Space, a 2023 initiative of the European Commission, has attempted to standardise consent and access rights, but compliance remains uneven and the underlying business models depend on data flows that residents may find difficult to refuse. Whether such schemes succeed will depend less on technological capacity than on regulatory will.

The two debates, ethical and infrastructural, are beginning to converge. A 2023 report by the International Transport Forum suggests that the most consequential ethical decisions in autonomous mobility may not concern the rare trolley scenario but rather the everyday allocation of street space: which kerbs are reserved for shared shuttles, which for private autonomous cars, which for cycling and which for pedestrians. The allocation, once made, tends to be sticky, and earlier transport revolutions, from the streetcar to the freeway, suggest that initial layouts can shape urban form for half a century. The forum's recommendation, that kerb-allocation rules be made explicit and reviewable rather than emerging implicitly from market forces, has gained traction among European city networks.

What appears, on balance, is a conversation that has matured. The early years of autonomous-vehicle discussion were dominated by spectacular thought experiments. More recent contributions have moved toward the unglamorous middle ground of perception engineering, subscription economics, kerb regulation and data governance. None of these are settled. Yet the shift in focus, from the rare and dramatic to the routine and consequential, may itself be the most useful outcome of the past decade of research, and one which the next decade of policy will be obliged to inherit.

audio_scripts.text: Right, good morning everyone, welcome to the Westport Intermodal Hub orientation tour. I'm Ling Cheng-Holloway, passenger-experience coordinator, and I'm gonna walk you through the building before your first commuter shift. [pause:3s] Let's start with orientation. If you stand at the Main Concourse entrance and face the central atrium, the tram platforms are directly ahead — that's the open, glass-roofed area beyond the ticket gates. The coach bays are on the FAR side of the atrium, opposite the entrance, accessed by the elevated walkway. The intercity rail platforms run along the LEFT side of the atrium, parallel to the building axis. The bike-hire dock sits in the south-east corner, between the coach bays and the rail platforms — that's important because it's NOT between the tram platforms and the entrance, as the old layout had it. The taxi rank is OUTSIDE the building, on the RIGHT-hand side as you exit. Left luggage is tucked under the elevated walkway, directly below the coach bays. And the staff lounge — well, that's reached via the corridor immediately behind the information desk, which itself sits to the right of the Main Concourse entrance. [pause:3s] Now, a few operational points. The bike-hire dock USED TO open at six in the morning, NOW it opens at five-thirty, and from this October it'LL open at five sharp to match the early commuter rail. So for your shifts this autumn, that's a five-thirty start, NOT five and NOT six. [pause:3s] Regarding the cap on simultaneous coach departures: most bay configurations permit twelve coaches at once, but the Westport bay has been derated to eight for this quarter — though only the Westport bay carries that lower threshold; all other regional bays remain at twelve. [pause:3s] Wi-Fi password for staff devices changes on the twenty-second of August — sorry, the twenty-fifth. Please update on the twenty-fifth, not the twenty-second. [pause:3s] Right, on to fare zones. We operate a zonal pricing structure with three tiers. Now, you might hear older colleagues refer to these as "rings", "bands", or "shells" — that's legacy vocabulary from before the 2024 restructure. The currently approved internal term is "zone" — z-o-n-e. So when an older colleague says "outer ring" or "second band", that's the same concept as "Zone 2", but you should use "zone" in customer-facing comms. [pause:3s] And finally, who's our point of contact for accessibility queries? Most queries should go to the Customer Care desk on the ground floor, but accessibility-specific issues actually go to the dedicated Mobility Lead on the mezzanine — most passengers send those to Customer Care by mistake. So please remember: Mobility Lead for accessibility, kinda counter-intuitive, sorta, but that's the policy. [pause:3s] One last reflection — let me return to the orientation point I made at the very start. That layout I described — with the bike-hire dock between coach bays and rail platforms — that's the CURRENT post-2024 configuration. The pre-2024 schematic, which still appears in some staff manuals, placed the bike-hire dock between the tram platforms and the entrance. If a passenger waves an old schematic at you, please redirect them to the current dock location. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

3.notes: #14 Tense-shift NEW — three tenses cluster ("USED TO open at six", "NOW it opens at five-thirty", "FROM THIS OCTOBER it'll open at five"); item targets the FUTURE tense. Candidate confused by stem opener "From this October" must lock onto future tense, not present. #2 Self-correction implicit — speaker re-states "NOT five and NOT six" reinforcing tense distinction. #1 Paraphrase T1.

blocks.text: The claim that autonomous vehicles will revolutionise transportation within the next two decades has become almost an article of faith among technology commentators. While I largely agree that self-driving cars will reshape mobility, I would argue that the transformation is likely to be slower and more uneven than enthusiasts suggest.

It is the elimination of human error that supporters of autonomy most often emphasise, and rightly so. Drunk driving, fatigue and road rage cause a substantial share of fatal accidents, and a well-functioning autonomous fleet could, in principle, reduce such incidents dramatically. In addition, self-driving vehicles communicating with one another may smooth traffic flow and thereby alleviate congestion, particularly when integrated into a multimodal transport network that includes mass transit. The aviation industry, too, has demonstrated that automation can outperform humans in routine operations, lending plausibility to the broader vision.

However, several factors temper my optimism. For one, the regulatory frameworks needed to govern liability remain underdeveloped; if a driverless car causes a fatal crash, it is far from clear who bears responsibility — the manufacturer, the software vendor or the passenger. Furthermore, the cost of autonomous vehicles is likely to remain prohibitively high for ordinary commuters in developing economies, where low-cost carriers and motorcycles continue to shape daily travel. The deployment of such technology may therefore be confined to wealthy enclaves long before it becomes a viable alternative globally.

In conclusion, while I broadly agree that autonomous vehicles will transform certain segments of transport — particularly freight and ride-hailing in advanced economies — I doubt the change will be universal within twenty years. The technology is genuinely promising, but social, legal and economic obstacles are bound to slow its diffusion.

That autonomous vehicles will reshape the transport landscape within twenty years has become a widely repeated forecast, championed by manufacturers and policymakers alike. While I am inclined to agree that the technology is poised to deliver significant change, I would contest the assumption that this transformation will be either uniform or as rapid as commonly suggested.

The case for transformation rests on several robust pillars. The substitution of human error by sensor-driven precision could, on balance, slash the road fatality rate, particularly in jurisdictions where drunk-driving and fatigue dominate accident statistics. Equally consequential is the prospect of fleet-level coordination, in which autonomous vehicles communicate to smooth traffic flow and alleviate the gridlock that plagues every major metropolis. So significant is the projected efficiency gain that several transport economists now treat autonomy as a precondition for any genuinely multimodal urban network.

Yet a sober reading suggests the timeline is overly optimistic. The deployment of autonomous fleets presupposes regulatory clarity around liability — a question that remains substantially unresolved in most jurisdictions. Moreover, the affordability barrier is unlikely to disappear quickly: in emerging economies, where low-cost carriers and two-wheeled commuting still dominate, the rollout of premium autonomous vehicles risks deepening transport inequality rather than alleviating it. Were rural communities and budget-conscious commuters excluded from the benefits, the much-heralded revolution would, in practice, be confined to affluent enclaves.

In conclusion, I largely concur that autonomous vehicles will transform certain segments — long-haul freight, urban ride-hailing and possibly subsidised mass transit — yet I remain sceptical of universal adoption within two decades. The technological foundations are, to a considerable extent, in place; what remains uncertain is whether regulators, insurers and consumers will move at a comparable pace.

solutions.text: Phần A

1. Several cities are trialling AUTONOMOUS VEHICLES, hoping to cut down on accidents caused by driver error. --- AUTONOMOUS VEHICLES (noun phrase, plural) = xe tự lái; collocation: "fully autonomous vehicles", "trial autonomous vehicles"; lưu ý "autonomous" là tính từ, không viết "autonomy vehicle".

2. A new metro line could help ALLEVIATE the traffic problem in the capital, though it probably won't solve it completely. --- ALLEVIATE (verb) = làm giảm bớt (không phải loại bỏ hoàn toàn); collocation: "alleviate congestion/the pressure/a problem"; không nhầm với "eliminate".

3. After years of staying in the same job, she felt a growing sense of WANDERLUST, so she quit and bought a one-way ticket. --- WANDERLUST (noun, uncountable) = khao khát du lịch mãnh liệt; collocation: "a sense of wanderlust", "satisfy your wanderlust"; không dùng "a wanderlust" theo nghĩa đếm được.

4. In cities with proper cycle lanes, riding a bike is becoming a VIABLE alternative to driving to work. --- VIABLE (adjective) = khả thi, thực tế; collocation: "a viable alternative/option", "economically viable"; dễ nhầm chính tả với "visible".

5. The AVIATION industry has faced growing pressure to explain its large share of global carbon emissions. --- AVIATION (noun, uncountable) = ngành hàng không; collocation: "the aviation industry", "civil aviation"; chỉ ngành nói chung, không dùng cho một chuyến bay cụ thể.

6. Without continued investment in transport INFRASTRUCTURE, a country's economy will struggle to remain competitive in the long run. --- INFRASTRUCTURE (noun, uncountable) = hạ tầng; collocation: "transport infrastructure", "invest in infrastructure"; không có dạng số nhiều "infrastructures".

7. New rules are forcing car manufacturers to cut vehicle EMISSIONS released by their exhaust pipes. --- EMISSIONS (noun, plural) = khí thải; collocation: "cut/reduce vehicle emissions", "carbon emissions"; thường dùng số nhiều khi nói chung về khí thải phương tiện.

8. Drivers entering the city centre now have to pay a CONGESTION CHARGE designed specifically to discourage unnecessary car journeys during the day. --- CONGESTION CHARGE (noun phrase) = phí ùn tắc; collocation: "introduce/pay a congestion charge", "congestion charge zone"; luôn viết "charge" số ít dù áp dụng cho nhiều xe.

9. Local authorities are promoting SUSTAINABLE MOBILITY that meets people's needs today without damaging the environment for future generations. --- SUSTAINABLE MOBILITY (noun phrase) = giao thông bền vững; collocation: "promote/invest in sustainable mobility", "a sustainable mobility plan".

10. Bike-sharing schemes have quickly GAINED significant TRACTION in several major cities over the past few years. --- GAIN TRACTION (verbal phrase) = bắt đầu được ưa chuộng/chấp nhận; collocation: "gain significant traction", "fail to gain traction"; nghĩa bóng, không liên quan đến ma sát vật lý.

11. Whenever planners widen a motorway, the extra space triggers INDUCED DEMAND, with new traffic filling the gap almost immediately. --- INDUCED DEMAND (noun phrase) = nhu cầu phát sinh; collocation: "the theory of induced demand", "a classic case of induced demand"; hiện tượng mở đường lại kéo theo xe cộ tăng thêm.

12. Topic: Restricting Air Travel vs. Freedom of Movement

For Restriction: Aviation is one of the fastest-growing sources of greenhouse gases; higher taxes on flights would force people to use greener alternatives like high-speed rail; it curbs unnecessary short-haul flights.

Against Restriction: It violates the fundamental right to unfettered mobility; heavily penalises budget airlines and low-income travellers while the rich simply pay the tax; severely damages tourism-dependent economies.
Topic: Solving Urban Traffic Congestion
Solution 1 (Financial Deterrents): Imposing strict congestion charges during peak hours and raising parking fees in the city centre to discourage private car usage.
Solution 2 (Subsidisation): Governments must heavily subsidise mass transit to make it a more viable, cheaper, and faster alternative to driving.
Solution 3 (Infrastructure): Investing in a multimodal transport network, specifically prioritising dedicated bus lanes and pedestrian/cycling infrastructure over building new highways.

Ecotourism (Benefits): Promotes sustainable travel off the beaten track; revenue directly supports conservation efforts and indigenous communities; fosters genuine respect and cultural exchange.

Model Answer (Band 7.5-8.0, ~268 words)

The transport system I'd like to discuss is the Tokyo metropolitan network — which I had the chance to experience during a two-week trip in late 2024 — and which I'd argue without hesitation is the gold standard for mass transit globally.

What sets Tokyo apart is the sheer scale and integration of its multimodal infrastructure. The network comprises 13 subway lines operated by two companies, the extensive JR commuter rail, the Yamanote loop line, plus an intricate web of private suburban railways — collectively moving roughly 40 million passengers daily, which is more than the entire population of Canada.

Efficiency-wise, the statistics are almost comical: average delays on the Shinkansen bullet trains hover around 24 seconds annually, and during the morning peak, trains on the Yamanote line arrive every 2 to 2.5 minutes. What impressed me most, however, wasn't merely the punctuality but the seamlessness — a single IC card called Suica works across virtually every operator, including buses, taxis, and even vending machines.

Aesthetically, the stations are remarkably well-designed, with platform doors preventing accidents, multilingual signage, and intuitive colour-coding. Rarely have I navigated such a complex system with so little friction, even as a first-time visitor with no Japanese.

What made it particularly memorable, though, was the cultural dimension. Trains run in near-total silence — phone calls are taboo — fostering an oddly meditative commute that contrasts sharply with the chaotic gridlock of Hanoi I'm used to.

In essence, Tokyo demonstrates that with sufficient investment, technical precision, and civic discipline, public transport can be not merely functional but genuinely transformative — and it's a model the rest of us would do well to emulate.

blocks.text: Q1: Should private cars be banned in cities?

Point: While an outright ban on private cars in urban centres might seem politically untenable, I'd argue that aggressive restriction — short of total prohibition — is not only justified but increasingly inevitable.

Explain: The economic principle at play here is what transport economists call "induced demand": building more roads paradoxically generates more traffic rather than alleviating congestion, because cheaper, faster driving simply encourages more journeys. Cars also impose substantial negative externalities — pollution, accidents, parking land — that drivers themselves don't pay for.

Example: Oslo offers perhaps the most instructive example: between 2017 and 2019, the city removed virtually all on-street parking from its centre and dramatically expanded pedestrian zones, with the result that pedestrian traffic rose 10% and retail revenue actually increased, contradicting the usual business objections. Pontevedra in Spain went further, effectively pedestrianising its entire historic centre in 1999, and has since seen traffic-related deaths fall to zero. London's Ultra Low Emission Zone, meanwhile, cut NO2 levels by 44% in just three years.

Link: So while a blanket ban is probably politically unfeasible in most contexts, congestion charging combined with car-free zones represents a pragmatic path forward — and the cities that have moved boldly are reaping demonstrable rewards.
Q2: Are e-scooters helpful?
Point: E-scooters are, on balance, a useful addition to the urban mobility toolkit, though their net benefit depends heavily on how they're integrated and regulated.

Explain: The theoretical appeal is that they solve the "last-mile problem" — the gap between transit stops and final destinations — while producing zero tailpipe emissions. However, their actual environmental impact is complicated by short device lifespans and the carbon-intensive logistics of nightly battery swaps.

Example: Life-cycle research on shared e-scooters suggests that once manufacturing and operations are accounted for, their per-passenger-mile carbon footprint can rival or even exceed that of a diesel bus. Conversely, in cities like Paris, where infrastructure was rapidly built out with 700 kilometres of cycling lanes by 2023, e-scooters complemented rather than competed with public transit. That said, Paris ultimately banned shared scooters via referendum in 2023, citing safety concerns — 459 injuries that year alone.

Link: This suggests that e-scooters are neither the panacea their advocates claim nor the menace critics describe; their utility depends almost entirely on dedicated infrastructure and sensible regulation.
Q3: Will hyperloop become viable?
Point: Frankly, I remain deeply sceptical that hyperloop technology will achieve commercial viability within the next two decades, despite the considerable hype surrounding it.

Explain: The fundamental obstacles are not so much engineering as economic and political. Maintaining a near-vacuum tube over hundreds of kilometres while moving passenger pods at 1,000 km/h requires extraordinarily tight tolerances, and any breach — from earthquakes, sabotage, or even thermal expansion — could be catastrophic. The construction cost per kilometre is estimated at $40-100 million, which is comparable to high-speed rail but with vastly more technical risk.

Example: Virgin Hyperloop, founded with much fanfare in 2014, conducted exactly one passenger test in 2020 and then pivoted entirely to cargo before laying off most staff in 2023. Hyperloop One similarly collapsed in late 2023. By contrast, China's conventional high-speed rail network now exceeds 45,000 kilometres, having been built in roughly the same time, and reliably operates at 350 km/h — fast enough for most realistic intercity needs.

Link: Ultimately, while it's possible that hyperloop may eventually find a niche on specific high-value corridors, conventional rail and possibly maglev are likely to remain the workhorses of intercity travel — hyperloop appears, for now, to be a solution in search of a problem.

4. Transcript (≈600 words)
> Right. Today I want to dismantle a stubborn fallacy in transport policy: the belief that we can build our way out of urban congestion. The geometry, frankly, does not cooperate.

> Begin with induced demand. The Texas A&M Transportation Institute and others have demonstrated that whenever a metropolitan highway is widened, new traffic materialises to fill the additional lanes within roughly three to five years. The mechanism is intuitive once stated: cheaper, faster driving encourages longer trips, more frequent trips and dispersed land use. The road network, in effect, generates the very traffic it was built to relieve. The implication is uncomfortable for politicians fond of ribbon-cuttings: lane expansion is, in the long run, self-defeating.

> Now, mass transit. A two-car-wide bus lane carrying articulated coaches moves roughly eight thousand passengers per hour; the same width devoted to private cars manages perhaps two thousand. A heavy-rail metro line can shift well over forty thousand. This is the stubborn arithmetic of urban capacity. Heavily subsidising rail, light rail and bus rapid transit is therefore not charity — it is engineering pragmatism.

> Finally, autonomous vehicles. The technology is genuinely impressive, and proponents promise reductions in road deaths and road rage. But the policy concern is rebound. If autonomous cars become a comfortable mobile office, commuters will tolerate vastly longer journeys, exacerbating sprawl rather than easing it. Without road-pricing, autonomy may simply scale up the very problem it claims to solve.

Before we reach that policy stack, though, I want to pre-empt an objection that always surfaces at this point — namely, that congestion charging is regressive, a tax on the working motorist while the wealthy simply absorb the fee. Well, the empirical record is more nuanced than the slogan suggests. Take Stockholm. When the city trialled its cordon charge in 2006, traffic across the cordon fell by roughly twenty percent, and — this is the part critics overlook — that reduction held steady years after the novelty wore off. [pause] More tellingly, public support inverted: opposition before the trial became a clear majority in favour once residents experienced quieter streets and faster buses. People, it turns out, dislike the idea of pricing far more than the reality of it.

Now, on the equity question specifically. The progressive design matters enormously. If you ring-fence the revenue and recycle it into the transit network — cheaper fares, more frequent services — the lowest-income decile, who disproportionately do not own cars, become net beneficiaries. London channels its charge revenue precisely this way. So the regressivity charge, um, depends entirely on what you do with the money, not on the levy itself.

Let me add one further wrinkle that rarely gets airtime: the role of parking. Donald Shoup, the UCLA economist, calculated that cruising for kerbside parking accounts for a startling share of downtown traffic — in some districts, up to thirty percent of vehicles circling are simply hunting for a space. [pause] Free or underpriced parking is, in effect, a hidden subsidy to driving that quietly sabotages every other intervention we make. Reform the parking, and you reform the demand curve upstream.

And there is a behavioural dimension too. Habit is sticky; commuters anchor to routines. The evidence from disruption studies — strikes, road closures — shows that when people are forced to try the alternative, a meaningful fraction never switch back. Which raises the central design question we now confront…

> Hence the policy stack we will examine after the break: congestion charging, bus-rapid-transit corridors, protected cycling networks, and serious investment in last-mile walkability. These work together; they fail alone. Now please turn to slide eleven…

Overall, the process is a linear yet branched sequence in which the battery, motor and chassis are produced separately before converging at final assembly.

Mô tả nhánh song song bằng bị động

Dùng 'Concurrently' + passive cho hai nhánh đồng thời.
Mô tả bước hội tụ và đầu ra cuối

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~184 từ)
The flow diagram outlines the eight-stage industrial process by which electric vehicles are manufactured, beginning with raw-material extraction and culminating in delivery to dealerships.

Overall, the process is a linear yet branched sequence in which the battery, the motor and the chassis are produced on parallel lines before converging at a single final-assembly point. The procedure is fully automated at its core and ends only once each vehicle has been tested and dispatched.

To begin with, lithium, cobalt and nickel are mined at remote sites and transported to a refining plant, where they are processed into cathode and anode materials. These inputs are subsequently fed into a cell-production line and grouped successively into modules and then into complete battery packs. Concurrently, on a separate line, the electric motor and the chassis are fabricated.

The three sub-assemblies are then brought together at a robotic final-assembly bay, where the vehicle is integrated. Once complete, each unit is subjected to quality testing and software calibration, after which it is stored at a logistics hub and ultimately dispatched to dealerships, reinforcing the global modal shift toward cleaner transport.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~189 từ)

The flow diagram delineates the eight discrete stages through which an electric vehicle is manufactured, commencing with the extraction of raw materials and culminating in its dispatch to dealerships.

Overall, what is most striking is the branched architecture of the process: rather than proceeding in a single chain, it splits into two parallel lines — one producing the battery and another the motor and chassis — which only converge at a robotic assembly point. The sequence is thus largely automated yet hinges on this critical moment of integration.

Initially, lithium, cobalt and nickel are mined and conveyed to a refining facility, where they are transformed into cathode and anode materials and assembled into cells. These cells are then grouped successively into modules and complete packs. Meanwhile, on an independent line, the electric motor and chassis are fabricated, so that the two streams advance simultaneously.

Not until the three sub-assemblies have been brought together at the robotic bay is the vehicle fully integrated. Thereafter, each unit undergoes quality testing and software calibration before being stored at a logistics hub and finally dispatched, thereby feeding the broader transition toward zero-emission mobility.
(g) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8
•  Band 8 mở Overview bằng nhận định về kiến trúc 'branched' (split into two parallel lines) thay vì chỉ liệt kê chuỗi tuyến tính như Band 7, thể hiện Task Achievement cao hơn.

•  Band 8 dùng đảo ngữ ('Not until the three sub-assemblies have been brought together is the vehicle fully integrated') và lexis kỹ thuật chính xác hơn ('delineates', 'discrete stages', 'conveyed', 'feeding the broader transition').
•  Band 8 kiểm soát sequencer và bị động liền mạch hơn ('Meanwhile ... so that ... Thereafter'), trong khi Band 7 lặp 'subsequently/then' nhiều hơn và cohesion phẳng hơn.
(h) Chiến lược làm bài (5 bước)
•  Đọc sơ đồ 30 giây để xác định đây là quy trình tuyến tính CÓ NHÁNH: tìm điểm rẽ nhánh (battery vs motor/chassis) và điểm hội tụ (final assembly) — đây là 'mỏ neo' cho Overview.
•  Viết Overview bằng 2 ý: (1) quy trình đi từ khai thác đến giao xe, (2) có hai nhánh song song hội tụ ở khâu lắp ráp — TUYỆT ĐỐI không nêu số liệu hay tên từng bước.
•  Mặc định dùng thể bị động ('is mined', 'are fabricated', 'is subjected to') vì tác nhân không quan trọng trong sơ đồ kỹ thuật.
•  Dùng dải sequencer đa dạng: Initially / To begin with > Subsequently > Concurrently / Meanwhile (cho nhánh song song) > Thereafter > finally — tránh lặp 'then ... then'.
•  Chia thân bài theo cụm logic (nhánh 1–4, hội tụ và đầu ra 5–8) chứ không kể lể từng bước rời rạc; gắn câu kết nhẹ về modal shift để khép mạch.

Đề bài.  Some people believe that autonomous (self-driving) vehicles will transform transportation in the next twenty years. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
(2) Từ vựng chủ đề (Band 8 topic & argument lexis)

blocks.text: (3) Ý tưởng hai chiều (Brainstorm)
Phía đồng tình (sẽ chuyển đổi mạnh):
•  Loại bỏ lỗi con người (say rượu, mệt mỏi, lái ẩu) có thể giảm mạnh tai nạn giao thông chết người.
•  Xe tự lái giao tiếp với nhau giúp làm mượt luồng giao thông và giảm ùn tắc tại đô thị lớn.
•  Hàng không đã chứng minh tự động hóa vượt con người ở các tác vụ lặp đi lặp lại — củng cố niềm tin vào tự hành.
Phía nghi ngờ (chuyển đổi chậm, không đồng đều):
•  Khung pháp lý về trách nhiệm khi xe tự lái gây tai nạn vẫn chưa rõ ràng (nhà sản xuất, hãng phần mềm hay hành khách?).
•  Chi phí quá cao khiến công nghệ chỉ phổ biến ở khu vực giàu, làm sâu thêm bất bình đẳng giao thông.
•  Ở nước đang phát triển, xe máy và hãng giá rẻ vẫn thống trị, nên triển khai bị giới hạn trong hai mươi năm.
(4) Gợi ý dàn bài — Introduction · Body 1 · Body 2 · Conclusion
•  Introduction — diễn giải nhận định 'xe tự hành sẽ chuyển đổi giao thông trong 20 năm'; thesis: phần lớn đồng tình nhưng chuyển đổi sẽ chậm và không đồng đều hơn dự báo.
•  Body 1 — vì sao có cơ sở để tin: loại bỏ lỗi con người, điều phối luồng giao thông, tiền lệ tự động hóa hàng không.
•  Body 2 — vì sao chuyển đổi bị giới hạn: khung trách nhiệm pháp lý chưa rõ, chi phí cao, thực tế xe máy/giá rẻ ở nước đang phát triển.
•  Conclusion — đồng tình một phần: chuyển đổi mạnh ở vận tải/gọi xe tại nước phát triển, nhưng khó phổ cập toàn cầu trong hai thập kỷ.

blocks.text: (6) Nâng cấp tục ngữ → diễn đạt học thuật

rows: "the technology is genuinely promising, yet its diffusion will be gradual and uneven"

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~281 words)

The claim that autonomous vehicles will revolutionise transportation within the next two decades has become almost an article of faith among technology commentators. While I largely agree that self-driving cars will reshape mobility, I would argue that the transformation is likely to be slower and more uneven than enthusiasts suggest.

It is the elimination of human error that supporters of autonomy most often emphasise, and rightly so. Drunk driving, fatigue and road rage cause a substantial share of fatal accidents, and a well-functioning autonomous fleet could, in principle, reduce such incidents dramatically. In addition, self-driving vehicles communicating with one another may smooth traffic flow and thereby alleviate congestion, particularly when integrated into a multimodal transport network that includes mass transit. The aviation industry, too, has demonstrated that automation can outperform humans in routine operations, lending plausibility to the broader vision.

However, several factors temper my optimism. For one, the regulatory frameworks needed to govern liability remain underdeveloped; if a driverless car causes a fatal crash, it is far from clear who bears responsibility — the manufacturer, the software vendor or the passenger. Furthermore, the cost of autonomous vehicles is likely to remain prohibitively high for ordinary commuters in developing economies, where low-cost carriers and motorcycles continue to shape daily travel. The deployment of such technology may therefore be confined to wealthy enclaves long before it becomes a viable alternative globally.

In conclusion, while I broadly agree that autonomous vehicles will transform certain segments of transport — particularly freight and ride-hailing in advanced economies — I doubt the change will be universal within twenty years. The technology is genuinely promising, but social, legal and economic obstacles are bound to slow its diffusion.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~283 words)

That autonomous vehicles will reshape the transport landscape within twenty years has become a widely repeated forecast, championed by manufacturers and policymakers alike. While I am inclined to agree that the technology is poised to deliver significant change, I would contest the assumption that this transformation will be either uniform or as rapid as commonly suggested.

The case for transformation rests on several robust pillars. The substitution of human error by sensor-driven precision could, on balance, slash the road fatality rate, particularly in jurisdictions where drunk-driving and fatigue dominate accident statistics. Equally consequential is the prospect of fleet-level coordination, in which autonomous vehicles communicate to smooth traffic flow and alleviate the gridlock that plagues every major metropolis. So significant is the projected efficiency gain that several transport economists now treat autonomy as a precondition for any genuinely multimodal urban network.

Yet a sober reading suggests the timeline is overly optimistic. The deployment of autonomous fleets presupposes regulatory clarity around liability — a question that remains substantially unresolved in most jurisdictions. Moreover, the affordability barrier is unlikely to disappear quickly: in emerging economies, where low-cost carriers and two-wheeled commuting still dominate, the rollout of premium autonomous vehicles risks deepening transport inequality rather than alleviating it. Were rural communities and budget-conscious commuters excluded from the benefits, the much-heralded revolution would, in practice, be confined to affluent enclaves.

In conclusion, I largely concur that autonomous vehicles will transform certain segments — long-haul freight, urban ride-hailing and possibly subsidised mass transit — yet I remain sceptical of universal adoption within two decades. The technological foundations are, to a considerable extent, in place; what remains uncertain is whether regulators, insurers and consumers will move at a comparable pace.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc cao cấp dày đặc hơn: đảo ngữ ('So significant is the projected efficiency gain that ...', 'Were rural communities ... excluded ...') và nominalisation ('the substitution of human error by sensor-driven precision', 'the deployment of autonomous fleets'), trong khi Band 7 chỉ dùng một cleft.

•  Band 8 nâng lexis lên bậc Band 8 ('sensor-driven precision', 'road fatality rate', 'gridlock', 'transport inequality') và giữ register kinh tế-giao thông nhất quán, thay cho cụm hơi đời thường như 'article of faith', 'rightly so' ở Band 7.

•  Band 8 lập luận sắc hơn ở phần phản biện (phân biệt rõ vận tải/gọi xe sẽ đổi vs phổ cập toàn cầu khó xảy ra) và cohesion mượt hơn ('Equally consequential is ...', 'Yet a sober reading suggests ...'), nâng Coherence & Task Response một bậc.

Xe tự lái là phương tiện có thể di chuyển mà không cần người điều khiển.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Many cities are trialling **autonomous vehicles** in an attempt to reduce accidents caused by human error.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Auto' (tự động) cộng với 'nomos' (tự quản) tạo thành xe 'tự quản', tức là xe tự lái không cần người điều khiển.
vocabulary.common_error: Người học hay quên 's' ở 'vehicles' hoặc viết 'autonomy vehicle' thay vì 'autonomous vehicle' (tính từ, không phải danh từ).
vocabulary.definition_en: cars or trucks capable of driving themselves without human intervention
vocabulary.definition_vi: xe tự lái, phương tiện tự hành không cần người điều khiển
vocabulary.example: Many cities are trialling autonomous vehicles in an attempt to reduce accidents caused by human error.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Auto' (tự động) + 'nomos' (luật, tự quản) → xe 'tự quản', tự lái không cần người.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Ùn tắc giao thông là tình trạng đường quá tải xe cộ khiến việc di chuyển bị chậm nghiêm trọng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Traffic **congestion** in the city centre gets so bad during rush hour that commuters often arrive an hour late.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Liên tưởng âm 'gest' trong congestion giống từ 'nghẹt' trong tiếng Việt, tức là đường bị nghẹt cứng vì quá nhiều xe.
vocabulary.common_error: Trong giao thông, nói *traffic congestion* hoặc *congestion on the roads*; không dùng *many congestions* trong nghĩa chung.
vocabulary.definition_en: the state of being so overcrowded with vehicles that movement is severely slowed
vocabulary.definition_vi: tình trạng ùn tắc, quá tải phương tiện khiến giao thông di chuyển rất chậm
vocabulary.example: Traffic congestion in the city centre gets so bad during rush hour that commuters often arrive an hour late.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung một con đường 'nghẹt' (con-GEST giống 'nghẹt') đầy xe cộ không nhúc nhích được.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Alleviate nghĩa là làm giảm bớt mức độ nghiêm trọng của một vấn đề, không phải loại bỏ hoàn toàn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Building a new metro line could help **alleviate** traffic congestion in the capital.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Nghe 'alleviate' giống 'a lever' (đòn bẩy) - dùng đòn bẩy để nâng bớt gánh nặng của vấn đề, tức là làm nó nhẹ đi.
vocabulary.common_error: Dễ nhầm 'alleviate' (làm giảm nhẹ) với 'eliminate' (loại bỏ hoàn toàn) — alleviate không có nghĩa là giải quyết dứt điểm.
vocabulary.definition_en: to make a problem less severe, intense, or serious; to relieve
vocabulary.definition_vi: làm giảm bớt, xoa dịu một vấn đề nghiêm trọng
vocabulary.example: Building a new metro line could help alleviate traffic congestion in the capital.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'A-LEVI-ate' nghe giống 'a lever' (đòn bẩy) giúp nâng bớt gánh nặng của vấn đề lên, tức là làm nhẹ đi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Wanderlust là niềm khao khát mãnh liệt muốn đi du lịch và khám phá thế giới.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Her **wanderlust** led her to backpack through fifteen countries before she turned twenty-five.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ghép 'wander' (lang thang) với 'lust' (khao khát mãnh liệt) để nhớ nghĩa là khao khát được đi khắp nơi.
vocabulary.common_error: Wanderlust là danh từ không đếm được, không dùng 'a wanderlust' theo nghĩa đếm số lần.
vocabulary.definition_en: a strong, irresistible desire to travel and explore the world
vocabulary.definition_vi: niềm khao khát mãnh liệt được đi du lịch, khám phá thế giới
vocabulary.example: Her wanderlust led her to backpack through fifteen countries before she turned twenty-five.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Wander' (lang thang) + 'lust' (khao khát mãnh liệt) → khao khát được lang thang khắp nơi.

Viable nghĩa là khả thi, có thể thực hiện thành công trên thực tế.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Cycling is becoming a **viable** alternative to driving in cities with dedicated bike lanes.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Via' trong tiếng Latin nghĩa là 'con đường', nên 'viable' là lựa chọn có đường đi được, tức là khả thi.
vocabulary.common_error: Không nhầm 'viable' (khả thi) với 'visible' (nhìn thấy được) - hai từ có chính tả gần giống nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: capable of working successfully; feasible and practical as an alternative
vocabulary.definition_vi: khả thi, có thể thực hiện được một cách thực tế
vocabulary.example: Cycling is becoming a viable alternative to driving in cities with dedicated bike lanes.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Via' nghĩa là 'con đường' trong tiếng Latin → một lựa chọn 'có đường đi', tức là khả thi để thực hiện.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Commuters là những người thường xuyên di chuyển quãng đường xa giữa nhà và nơi làm việc.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> During rush hour, thousands of **commuters** cram onto the metro to get to work on time.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Liên tưởng 'commute' là hành trình 'thông đi thông về' mỗi ngày giữa nhà và chỗ làm.
vocabulary.common_error: Commuters là người, còn 'commute' là động từ chỉ hành động di chuyển - không dùng lẫn hai từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: people who travel a considerable distance regularly between home and work
vocabulary.definition_vi: người đi làm/đi học thường xuyên với quãng đường xa
vocabulary.example: During rush hour, thousands of commuters cram onto the metro to get to work on time.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Commute' nghe gần giống 'thông đi thông về' mỗi ngày giữa nhà và nơi làm việc.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Multimodal nghĩa là đa phương thức, kết hợp nhiều loại hình vận chuyển khác nhau.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A **multimodal** transport system that links buses, trains and bike-sharing schemes can significantly cut car usage.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ghép 'multi' (nhiều) với 'modal' (phương thức) để nhớ nghĩa là kết hợp nhiều phương thức vận chuyển.
vocabulary.common_error: Không viết tách 'multi modal' thành hai từ; đây là một tính từ ghép viết liền.
vocabulary.definition_en: involving several different methods or means, especially of transport
vocabulary.definition_vi: đa phương thức, kết hợp nhiều hình thức vận chuyển khác nhau
vocabulary.example: A multimodal transport system that links buses, trains and bike-sharing schemes can significantly cut car usage.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The **aviation** industry has come under scrutiny for its significant contribution to global carbon emissions.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Latin 'avi' nghĩa là 'chim', gợi liên tưởng đến việc bay trên trời, chính là ngành hàng không.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hạ tầng giao thông là hệ thống cơ sở vật chất nền tảng như đường sá, cầu cống, đường sắt.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Investing in transport **infrastructure**, such as high-speed rail, is essential for reducing regional inequality.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Infra' nghĩa là 'bên dưới', ghép với 'structure' (cấu trúc) tạo thành nền tảng nằm bên dưới nâng đỡ cả hệ thống.
vocabulary.common_error: Infrastructure là danh từ không đếm được, không dùng 'infrastructures' hoặc 'an infrastructure'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the basic physical systems and structures needed for a society or system to operate, such as roads, bridges and railways
vocabulary.definition_vi: hạ tầng giao thông, hệ thống cơ sở vật chất nền tảng
vocabulary.example: Investing in transport infrastructure, such as high-speed rail, is essential for reducing regional inequality.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Infra' nghĩa là 'bên dưới' + 'structure' (cấu trúc) → những cấu trúc nền tảng nằm bên dưới, hỗ trợ cả hệ thống.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khí thải là các chất, đặc biệt là khí, được thải ra môi trường từ việc đốt nhiên liệu.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Governments are introducing stricter regulations to cut vehicle **emissions** and improve air quality in cities.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ghép 'e-' (ra ngoài) với 'mission' (nhiệm vụ) để hình dung khí thải đang thoát ra ngoài không khí.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Emissions' thường dùng ở số nhiều khi nói chung về khí thải phương tiện; dạng số ít 'emission' ít phổ biến hơn trong ngữ cảnh này.
vocabulary.definition_en: substances, especially gases, that are released into the air, often as a by-product of burning fuel
vocabulary.definition_vi: khí thải, chất thải ra môi trường
vocabulary.example: Governments are introducing stricter regulations to cut vehicle emissions and improve air quality in cities.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'E-' (ra ngoài) + 'mission' (nhiệm vụ) → tưởng tượng khí thải đang 'thực hiện nhiệm vụ' thoát ra ngoài không khí.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Phí ùn tắc là khoản phí thu từ tài xế khi vào khu vực đô thị đông đúc nhằm giảm ùn tắc.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> London and Stockholm both introduced a **congestion charge** that significantly reduced the number of cars entering the city centre.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Nhớ đến London thu phí để chống ùn tắc khi xe cộ đi vào trung tâm thành phố.
vocabulary.common_error: Congestion charge là cụm danh từ ghép, luôn viết 'charge' ở số ít dù áp dụng cho nhiều xe.
vocabulary.definition_en: a fee charged to drivers for entering a busy urban area, designed to reduce traffic
vocabulary.definition_vi: phí ùn tắc, khoản phí thu để giảm ùn tắc giao thông ở khu vực đông đúc
vocabulary.example: London and Stockholm both introduced a congestion charge that significantly reduced the number of cars entering the city centre.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Liên tưởng London thu 'phí' (charge) để chống 'ùn tắc' (congestion) khi xe vào trung tâm thành phố.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Giao thông bền vững là hình thức di chuyển đáp ứng nhu cầu hiện tại mà không gây hại cho môi trường tương lai.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> City planners are promoting **sustainable mobility** by expanding cycle lanes and electric bus networks.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ghép 'sustain' (duy trì lâu dài) với 'mobility' (khả năng di chuyển) để nhớ đây là cách di chuyển bền vững với môi trường.
vocabulary.common_error: Không thu hẹp *sustainable mobility* chỉ thành xe điện; khái niệm còn gồm đi bộ, xe đạp, giao thông công cộng và giảm nhu cầu di chuyển.
vocabulary.definition_en: forms of transport and travel that meet current needs without harming the environment for future generations
vocabulary.definition_vi: giao thông bền vững, hình thức di chuyển không gây hại môi trường lâu dài
vocabulary.example: City planners are promoting sustainable mobility by expanding cycle lanes and electric bus networks.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Sustain' (duy trì lâu dài) + 'mobility' (khả năng di chuyển) → di chuyển theo cách có thể duy trì mãi mà không hại môi trường.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tắc nghẽn cứng là tình trạng giao thông nặng đến mức các phương tiện hoàn toàn không thể di chuyển.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Rush-hour **gridlock** in the downtown area can leave commuters stuck for over an hour.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Grid' (mạng lưới ô vuông đường phố) bị 'lock' (khoá cứng) - toàn bộ mạng lưới đường phố tê liệt hoàn toàn.
vocabulary.common_error: Gridlock nghiêm trọng hơn 'congestion' - gridlock nghĩa là xe hoàn toàn đứng yên, không chỉ chậm lại.
vocabulary.definition_en: a situation in which traffic is so heavy that vehicles cannot move at all
vocabulary.definition_vi: tắc nghẽn cứng, tình trạng xe cộ hoàn toàn không thể di chuyển
vocabulary.example: Rush-hour gridlock in the downtown area can leave commuters stuck for over an hour.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Grid' (lưới ô vuông đường phố) bị 'lock' (khoá cứng) → cả mạng lưới đường phố bị khoá cứng, không xe nào nhúc nhích.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Pedestrianise nghĩa là biến một khu vực hoặc con phố thành nơi chỉ dành cho người đi bộ, cấm xe cộ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Oslo **pedestrianised** much of its city centre, removing on-street parking and boosting pedestrian traffic.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ghép 'pedestrian' (người đi bộ) với hậu tố '-ise' (biến thành) để nhớ nghĩa là biến phố thành khu đi bộ.
vocabulary.common_error: Chú ý chính tả Anh-Anh 'pedestrianise' (không phải 'pedestrianize' theo kiểu Mỹ) để giữ nhất quán British spelling.
vocabulary.definition_en: to convert a street or area so that only pedestrians, not vehicles, are allowed
vocabulary.definition_vi: biến thành khu đi bộ, cấm xe cộ ra vào một khu vực
vocabulary.example: Oslo pedestrianised much of its city centre, removing on-street parking and boosting pedestrian traffic.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Pedestrian' (người đi bộ) + '-ise' (biến thành) → biến một con phố thành nơi chỉ dành cho người đi bộ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Decarbonise nghĩa là khử carbon, tức là giảm hoặc loại bỏ khí thải carbon khỏi một hệ thống hay ngành.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Decarbonising** transport will require a rapid shift towards electric vehicles and renewable energy sources.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ghép 'de-' (loại bỏ) với 'carbon' và '-ise' (làm cho) để nhớ nghĩa là làm cho hệ thống loại bỏ khí carbon.
vocabulary.common_error: Chú ý chính tả Anh-Anh 'decarbonise' (không phải 'decarbonize') để đồng nhất với các từ '-ise' khác trong bài.
vocabulary.definition_en: to reduce or remove carbon dioxide emissions from a process, industry or system
vocabulary.definition_vi: khử carbon, loại bỏ hoặc giảm khí thải carbon
vocabulary.example: Decarbonising transport will require a rapid shift towards electric vehicles and renewable energy sources.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'De-' (loại bỏ) + 'carbon' (carbon) + '-ise' (làm cho) → làm cho hệ thống loại bỏ carbon.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Gain traction nghĩa là một ý tưởng hay xu hướng bắt đầu được nhiều người ủng hộ và chấp nhận.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> E-scooter schemes have **gained** significant **traction** in European cities as a solution to the last-mile problem.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Bánh xe cần lực bám đường (traction) để lăn đi; một ý tưởng cũng cần 'lực bám' để lan rộng và được chấp nhận.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Traction' vốn nghĩa gốc là lực bám/kéo (của bánh xe); trong cụm này nó mang nghĩa bóng là 'sự ủng hộ', không liên quan trực tiếp đến ma sát vật lý.
vocabulary.definition_en: to start to become popular, accepted or supported
vocabulary.definition_vi: bắt đầu được ưa chuộng, được chấp nhận rộng rãi
vocabulary.example: E-scooter schemes have gained significant traction in European cities as a solution to the last-mile problem.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung bánh xe cần 'traction' (lực bám đường) để lăn đi - một ý tưởng cũng cần lực bám để 'lăn' vào cộng đồng và được chấp nhận.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hit the road là thành ngữ nghĩa là lên đường, bắt đầu một chuyến đi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We packed the car early in the morning and **hit the road** before the traffic got heavy.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Tưởng tượng bàn chân vừa 'đập' xuống mặt đường ngay khoảnh khắc bắt đầu lên đường.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Hit the road' không có nghĩa đen là 'đánh vào đường'; đây là thành ngữ chỉ hành động bắt đầu di chuyển.
vocabulary.definition_en: to begin a journey, especially by car
vocabulary.definition_vi: lên đường, bắt đầu một chuyến đi
vocabulary.example: We packed the car early in the morning and hit the road before the traffic got heavy.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Tưởng tượng bàn chân 'đập' (hit) xuống mặt đường (road) ngay khi bắt đầu bước ra khỏi nhà để lên đường.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Itchy feet là thành ngữ diễn tả cảm giác nôn nao, muốn đi du lịch hoặc trải nghiệm điều mới.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> After six months in the same city, she started getting **itchy feet** and began planning her next trip.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Bàn chân như đang 'ngứa ngáy', thôi thúc bạn phải bước đi chứ không thể ngồi yên một chỗ.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Itchy feet' luôn dùng ở dạng số nhiều 'feet', không nói 'an itchy foot' theo nghĩa thành ngữ này.
vocabulary.definition_en: a strong urge or restlessness to travel or try something new
vocabulary.definition_vi: cảm giác nôn nao muốn đi du lịch hoặc thay đổi, khó ngồi yên một chỗ
vocabulary.example: After six months in the same city, she started getting itchy feet and began planning her next trip.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Bàn chân 'ngứa ngáy' (itchy) như đang thôi thúc bạn phải bước đi, không thể đứng yên một chỗ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Live out of a suitcase là thành ngữ chỉ lối sống di chuyển liên tục, không có nơi ở cố định.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> As a flight attendant, she practically **lives out of a suitcase**, spending only a few nights a month at home.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình dung một người luôn để đồ trong vali thay vì cất vào tủ, vì họ chẳng bao giờ ở một chỗ đủ lâu.
collocations: live out of a suitcase for months
tired of living out of a suitcase
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là thành ngữ mang nghĩa bóng chỉ lối sống di chuyển liên tục, không phải nghĩa đen là 'sống bên trong vali'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to travel or move frequently, without a settled, permanent home
vocabulary.definition_vi: sống nay đây mai đó, thường xuyên di chuyển mà không có nhà ổn định
vocabulary.example: As a flight attendant, she practically lives out of a suitcase, spending only a few nights a month at home.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung một người luôn để đồ trong vali (suitcase) thay vì cất vào tủ, vì họ không bao giờ ở một chỗ đủ lâu.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
In the driver's seat là thành ngữ nghĩa là nắm quyền kiểm soát hoặc làm chủ một tình huống.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> With the new transport bill passed, the mayor is firmly **in the driver's seat** when it comes to city planning.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Người ngồi ở ghế lái là người quyết định hướng đi của cả chiếc xe, giống như người đang kiểm soát tình huống.
collocations: put someone in the driver's seat
vocabulary.common_error: Thành ngữ này dùng nghĩa bóng để chỉ quyền kiểm soát nói chung, không nhất thiết liên quan đến việc thực sự lái xe.
vocabulary.definition_en: to be in control of a situation or in charge of decision-making
vocabulary.definition_vi: nắm quyền kiểm soát, làm chủ tình hình
vocabulary.example: With the new transport bill passed, the mayor is firmly in the driver's seat when it comes to city planning.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Người ngồi ở 'ghế lái' (driver's seat) là người điều khiển hướng đi của cả chiếc xe, cũng như người kiểm soát tình huống.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Backseat driver là thành ngữ chỉ người hay xen vào góp ý, chỉ trích không được yêu cầu.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> My uncle is such a **backseat driver** during family meetings, constantly telling the project manager what to do.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Tưởng tượng người ngồi ghế sau liên tục chỉ đạo tài xế phải rẽ đâu, dù không phải người thực sự lái xe.
vocabulary.common_error: Thành ngữ này thường mang sắc thái tiêu cực, chỉ trích người can thiệp không đúng lúc, không chỉ đơn thuần người ngồi ghế sau xe.
vocabulary.definition_en: someone who annoyingly gives unwanted advice or criticism, especially about how something should be done
vocabulary.definition_vi: người hay xen vào chỉ trích, góp ý không được yêu cầu (thường ví như người ngồi ghế sau chỉ tài xế lái xe)
vocabulary.example: My uncle is such a backseat driver during family meetings, constantly telling the project manager what to do.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Tưởng tượng người ngồi ghế sau (backseat) liên tục chỉ đạo tài xế phải rẽ đâu, dù không phải người lái xe.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Induced demand là hiện tượng mở rộng hạ tầng đường sá lại vô tình kéo theo lượng xe cộ và ùn tắc mới.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The lecturer explained **induced demand**: widening the motorway simply encouraged more people to drive, and congestion returned within a year.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Induce' nghĩa là 'gây ra' - mở đường rộng hơn lại vô tình gây ra nhu cầu lái xe nhiều hơn, một nghịch lý thú vị.
collocations: a classic case of induced demand
vocabulary.common_error: Induced demand không có nghĩa là 'nhu cầu bị ép buộc' theo nghĩa đen mà là nhu cầu mới được 'sinh ra' bởi chính giải pháp ban đầu.
vocabulary.definition_en: the phenomenon whereby increasing road capacity encourages more people to drive, ultimately generating new traffic
vocabulary.definition_vi: nhu cầu phát sinh, hiện tượng mở rộng đường sá lại kéo theo lượng xe tăng thêm
vocabulary.example: The lecturer explained induced demand: widening the motorway simply encouraged more people to drive, and congestion returned within a year.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Induce' nghĩa là 'gây ra, tạo ra' → mở đường rộng hơn lại 'gây ra' (induce) nhu cầu lái xe nhiều hơn, một nghịch lý giao thông.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Last-mile là chặng cuối ngắn của hành trình, nối từ trạm giao thông công cộng đến điểm đến cuối cùng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> E-scooters have become a popular solution to the **last-mile** problem, helping commuters get from the station to their office.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình dung 'dặm cuối cùng' từ trạm xe buýt về đến tận cửa nhà - đoạn ngắn nhưng thường bị bỏ sót khi quy hoạch giao thông.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Last-mile' không có nghĩa đen là đúng một dặm; nó chỉ chặng cuối ngắn của hành trình dù độ dài thực tế có thể khác.
vocabulary.definition_en: relating to the final, short segment of a journey between a public transit stop and the traveller's actual destination
vocabulary.definition_vi: chặng cuối, đoạn đường ngắn cuối cùng từ trạm giao thông công cộng đến điểm đến thực sự
vocabulary.example: E-scooters have become a popular solution to the last-mile problem, helping commuters get from the station to their office.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung 'dặm cuối cùng' (last mile) từ trạm xe buýt về đến tận cửa nhà - đoạn ngắn nhưng hay bị bỏ sót trong quy hoạch.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Off the beaten track là thành ngữ chỉ những nơi xa xôi, hẻo lánh, ít khách du lịch ghé thăm.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Ecotourism encourages travellers to explore destinations **off the beaten track** rather than crowding into cities like Venice or Barcelona.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Beaten track' là con đường mòn bị giẫm nhẵn bởi đông người qua lại; 'off' nó nghĩa là tránh xa con đường đông đúc đó.
collocations: a destination off the beaten track
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm này luôn giữ nguyên dạng 'off the beaten track', không chia động từ hay đổi thứ tự từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: remote or unusual; not visited by many tourists or travellers
vocabulary.definition_vi: xa xôi, hẻo lánh, ít người biết đến hoặc ít khách du lịch ghé thăm
vocabulary.example: Ecotourism encourages travellers to explore destinations off the beaten track rather than crowding into cities like Venice or Barcelona.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Beaten track' là con đường mòn đã bị 'giẫm' (beaten) nhẵn bởi nhiều người đi qua; 'off' nó nghĩa là tránh xa lối mòn đông đúc đó.
